# Boilers and the safety valve (`safety_valve_boiler`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by atmospheric_pressure, rolling_mill, puddling_wrought_iron, copper_bronze
- Core idea: When a boiler makes steam faster than it can escape, pressure can exceed the strength of the shell. A relief valve must both open at its set pressure and discharge steam at least as fast as the fire can produce it. Papin used a weighted lever to hold a valve on its seat; its load determined when steam pressure lifted the valve. A working boiler also needs a way to see the water level (two try cocks, later a glass gauge) and a feed pump, because fire on a plate not covered by water makes it red hot and weak. The force trying to burst a cylindrical shell grows with pressure times diameter, so strong boilers are small in diameter, round, of riveted wrought-iron or copper plate, with flat surfaces stayed. Newcomen's copper and lead boilers held 1 to 2 pounds per square inch above the air, Watt's about 5, Trevithick's Cornish boiler 40 to 50. The danger is the hot water more than the steam: when a shell tears, some of the pressurised hot water flashes into a much larger volume of steam.
- Pitfalls:
  - Tying down or overloading the safety valve to get more power; the classic cause of explosions
  - Letting the water fall below the fire line, then pumping cold water onto the overheated plate
  - Cast iron, soldered seams or flat unstayed plates for anything above a few pounds of pressure
  - Relying on a relief valve to protect an exposed firebox crown. Low water can weaken the metal even at normal pressure; a fusible plug is a separate historical safeguard
  - Ignoring scale from hard water, which insulates the plate until it overheats
- History: greece: 1st c. AD – Hero's small closed boilers for temple tricks; no safety device; europe: 1679 – Denis Papin's digester (pressure cooker) with weighted lever safety valve, published 1681; 1712 Newcomen's low-pressure haystack boiler; 1803 Trevithick adds the fusible plug after the Greenwich explosion; 1812 Cornish boiler with internal flue; 1827–1829 multi-tube boilers of Séguin and of Booth and Stephenson; 1844 Lancashire boiler; americas: 1830s – Franklin Institute investigates steamboat boiler explosions; 1838 and 1852 federal steamboat acts introduce and strengthen federal inspection
- Read:
  - Denis Papin, A New Digester or Engine for Softning Bones (1681)
  - Richard L. Hills, Power from Steam: A History of the Stationary Steam Engine (1989)
  - John G. Burke, Bursting Boilers and the Federal Power, Technology and Culture 7 (1966)
